source_text: Μειρακίοις δὲ γυμνάσιον ἀπόχρη, κἂν βαλανεῖον παρῇ· καὶ γὰρ καὶ ταῦτα τοῖς ἀνδράσι παντὸς μᾶλλον πρὸ τῶν λουτρῶν ἐγκρῖναι οὐ φαῦλον ἴσως, ἔχοντά τι χρήσιμον τοῖς νέοις πρὸς ὑγίειαν, σπουδήν τε καὶ φιλοτιμίαν ἐντιθέντα οὐχὶ εὐεξίας μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ εὐψυχίας ἐπιμελεῖσθαι· ὃ δὴ γινόμενον ἄνευ τοῦ τῶν κρειττόνων ἔργων ἀποσπᾶσθαι χαρίεν καὶ οὐκ ἀλυσιτελές. οὐδὲ ἐνταῦθα ὑπεξαιρετέον τῆς κατὰ τὸ σῶμα διαπονήσεως τὰς γυναῖκας, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἐπὶ πάλην καὶ δρόμους παρακλητέον αὐτάς, ταλασιουργίᾳ δὲ γυμναστέον καὶ ἱστουργίᾳ καὶ τῷ παραστῆναι τῇ πεττούσῃ, εἰ δέοι. ἔτι δὲ αὐτουργικῶς προκομίζειν χρὴ ἐκ τοῦ ταμιείου τὰς γυναῖκας ὧν δεοίμεθα, καὶ τῷ μύλῳ προσελθεῖν οὐκ αἰσχρὸν αὐταῖς· οὐδὲ μὴν περὶ τοὔψον ἀσχολεῖσθαι, ὅπως θυμῆρες ᾖ τἀνδρί, ὄνειδος οἰκουρῷ γαμετῇ καὶ βοηθῷ. εἰ δὲ καὶ στρωμνὴν ἀνατινάξαι δι᾿ αὑτῆς καὶ ποτὸν ὀρέξαι διψῶντι τῷ γεγαμηκότι καὶ ὄψον παραθείη, εὐσχημονέστατα μεντἂν καὶ εἰς σώφρονα ὑγίειαν γυμνασθείη· τὴν τοιαύτην γυναῖκα ὁ παιδαγωγὸς ἀποδέχεται, ἣ »τοὺς πήχεις ἐκτενεῖ εἰς τὰ χρήσιμα, τὰς χεῖρας δὲ αὐτῆς ἐρείδεται εἰς ἄτρακτον· χεῖρας δὲ αὐτῆς διήνοιξεν πένητι, καρπὸν δὲ ἐξέτεινεν πτωχῷ«, τὴν καλλίστην διακονίαν οὐκ ἐπῃσχύνθη ζηλώσασα Σάρραν, ὑπουργῆσαι τοῖς ὁδοιπόροις. εἶπεν γὰρ αὐτῇ Ἀβραάμ· »σπεῦσον καὶ φύρασον τρία μέτρα σεμιδάλεως καὶ ποίησον ἐγκρυφίας.« »Ῥαχὴλ δὲ ἡ θυγάτηρ Λάβαν ἤρχετο«, φησί, »μετὰ τῶν προβάτων τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῆς.« καὶ οὐκ ἤρκει ταῦτα, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἀτυφίαν ἐκδιδάσκων προσεπήγαγεν· »αὕτη γὰρ ἔβοσκεν τὰ πρόβατα τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῆς.« καὶ μυρία ὅσα αἱ γραφαὶ ὀρέγουσιν εὐτελείας ἅμα καὶ αὐτουργίας, πρὸς δὲ καὶ γυμνασίων ὑποδείγματα. ἀνδρῶν δὲ οἳ μὲν γυμνοὶ καὶ πάλης μετεχόντων, οἳ δὲ καὶ σφαίρῃ τῇ μικρᾷ παιζόντων τὴν φαινίνδα παιδιὰν ἐν ἡλίῳ μάλιστα· ἄλλοις ὁ περίπατος αὐτάρκης ἀγρόνδε βαδίζουσιν ἢ εἰς ἄστυ κατιοῦσιν. εἰ δὲ καὶ σκαπάνης ἅψαιντο, οὐκ ἀγεννὲς τοῦτο παρεμπόρευμα οἰκονομικὸν γυμνασίου γεωργικοῦ. ἀλλὰ γὰρ μικροῦ δεῖν ἔλαθέν με [εἰπεῖν] ὁ Πιττακὸς ἐκεῖνος, ὅτι ἤληθεν ὁ Μιτυληναίων βασιλεὺς ἐνεργῷ γυμνασίῳ χρώμενος. καλὸν δὲ καὶ ὕδωρ ἀνιμῆσαι δι᾿ αὑτοῦ καὶ ξύλα διατεμεῖν, οἷς αὐτὸς χρήσεται. »Ἰακὼβ δὲ ἐποίμαινεν τὰ πρόβατα Λάβαν τὰ ὑπολειφθέντα«, σημεῖον ἔχων βασιλικὸν »ῥάβδον στυρακίνην«, ἐναλλάττειν μελετῶν διὰ τοῦ ξύλου ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον τὴν φύσιν. πολλοῖς δὲ ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε καὶ τὸ γεγωνὸς τῆς ἀναγνώσεως γυμνάσιόν ἐστιν. καὶ δὴ τά γε [καὶ] κατὰ πάλην, ἣν ἐνεκρίναμεν, μὴ φιλονεικίας ἀχρήστου παραλαμβανέσθω χάριν, εἰς δὲ ἱδρώτων ἀνδρωδῶν ἐκκρίσεις· καὶ οὔτι γε τὸ ἔντεχνον διαπονητέον, τὸ ἐπιδεικτικὸν αὐτῆς, τὰ δὲ ἀπὸ ὀρθῆς πάλης, ἀπ᾿ αὐχένων καὶ χειρῶν καὶ πλευρῶν ἐξειλήσεως· κοσμιωδεστέρα γὰρ καὶ ἀνδρωδεστέρα μετ᾿ εὐσχήμονος ῥώμης ἡ τοιαύτη διαπόνησις ὑγείας ἕνεκεν εὐχρήστου καὶ ὀνησιφόρου παραλαμβανομένη, οἱ δὲ ἄλλοι πόνοι γυμναστικῆς οὐκ ἐλευθέρων στάσεων μελέτην καταγγέλλοντες. πανταχοῦ δὲ τοῦ μέτρου στοχαστέον. ὡς γὰρ πόνους σιτίων ἡγεῖσθαι ἄριστον, οὕτως τὸ ὑπὲρ τὸ μέτρον πονεῖν καὶ κάκιστον καὶ κοπῶδες καὶ νοσοποιόν. οὔτ᾿ οὖν παντάπασιν ἀργὸν εἶναι χρὴ οὐδὲ μὴν παντελῶς ἐπίπονον. καθάπερ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῆς τροφῆς διεξεληλύθαμεν, παραπλησίως ἐν πᾶσι καὶ πανταχοῦ οὐ πρὸς ἡδυπάθειαν τετράφθαι καὶ ἀκόλαστον χρὴ δίαιταν οὐδ᾿ αὖ πρὸς τὴν ἐναντίαν τὴν ἄκρατον, ἀλλὰ τὴν μεταξὺ τούτων τὴν ἐμμελῆ τε καὶ σώφρονα καὶ καθαρὰν ἑκατέρας κακίας, τρυφῆς τε καὶ φειδωλίας. ἤδη δέ, ὡς καὶ πρόσθεν εἰρήκαμεν, ἄτυφον ἡ αὐτουργία γυμνάσιον καὶ τὸ ὑποδήσασθαί τινα αὐτὸν αὑτῷ καὶ τὸ ἀπονίψασθαι τὼ πόδε, πρὸς δὲ καὶ τὸ ἀληλιμμένον λίπα ἀνατρῖψαι αὑτόν· τὸ δὲ καὶ τὴν ἀμοιβὴν τὴν ἴσην ἀνταποδοῦναι τῷ τρίψαντι ἐναλλὰξ καὶ τοῦτο δικαιοσύνης ἐστὶ κοινωνικῆς τὸ γυμνάσιον καὶ παραδαρθεῖν φίλῳ νοσοῦντι καὶ ὑπουργῆσαι μὴ δυναμένῳ καὶ παραθεῖναι δεομένῳ. »καὶ παρέθηκεν αὐτοῖς«, φησίν, »Ἀβραὰμ τοῖς τρισὶν ἄριστον ὑπὸ τὸ δένδρον καὶ παρέστη ἐσθίουσιν αὐτοῖς.« καὶ ἡ ἁλεία, ὡς τῷ Πέτρῳ, εἰ σχολὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἀναγκαίων τῶν ἐν λόγῳ μαθημάτων ἄγοιμεν. αὕτη δὲ βελτίων ἡ ἄγρα, ἣν ἐχαρίσατο ὁ κύριος τῷ μαθητῇ, καθάπερ ἰχθῦς δι᾿ ὕδατος ἀνθρώπους ἁλιεύειν διδάξας.
pass_a_gloss: For young men, a gymnasium is sufficient, even if a bath is available; and indeed these things are more suitable for men before bathing, not being worthless, but having something useful for the young for health, and also for diligence and ambition, not only for elegance, but also for taking care of their souls; which is indeed pleasant and not unprofitable when done without being distracted from better works. And here, women should not be exempt from bodily exercise, but they should not be encouraged to wrestling and running, but rather to wool-working and weaving and to standing by the spinning woman if needed. And indeed, it is necessary for women to personally bring forth from the storehouse what we need, and for them to approach the mill is not shameful for them; nor should they be concerned about their hair, so that it may be a shame for the husband and a reproach for the house. If indeed a woman also knows how to spread out a bed and to give a drink to her thirsty husband and to serve a meal, she would be exercising in a most decent and sober way for health; such a woman the Pedagogue accepts, who 'stretches out her arms for useful things, and her hands she weaves into a spindle; and she opens her hands to the poor, and she stretches out fruit to the needy', not being ashamed to serve the travelers, imitating Sarah. For Abraham said to her, 'Hurry and knead three measures of fine flour and make cakes.' 'And Rachel, the daughter of Laban, was coming', it says, 'with the sheep of her father.' And it was not enough for her to do these things, but also, teaching humility, she added, 'For she was shepherding the sheep of her father.' And the scriptures encourage many things, such as frugality and personal labor, and also examples of exercise. Some men exercise naked and engage in wrestling, others play with a small ball, enjoying the pleasure of play in the sun; for others, walking is sufficient, whether they walk in the country or go to the city. And if they also engage in digging, this is not an ignoble accompaniment to economic exercise in farming. But I almost forgot to say that even Pittacus, the king of the Mytilenaeans, was strengthened by energetic exercise. It is also good to draw water by oneself and to cut wood, which one will use. 'And Jacob was pasturing the sheep of Laban that were left', having a royal sign, 'a staff of storax', and he was practicing to exchange the wood for the better nature. For many, even reading aloud is exercise. And indeed, the things concerning wrestling, which we have judged, should not be taken as useless rivalry, but rather as a manly and sweaty exercise; and not the artificial and showy kind, but the kind that comes from upright wrestling, from neck and hands and sides, which is more decent and manly with modest strength, taken for the sake of useful and beneficial health. But other gymnastic exercises declare the study of servile postures. Everywhere, one must consider measure. For just as it is best to consider the pains of food, so also to labor beyond measure is worst and troublesome and disease-causing. Therefore, one should not be completely idle nor completely laborious. Just as we have discussed concerning food, similarly in all things and everywhere, one should not be turned towards pleasure and intemperance, nor towards the opposite, the extreme, but rather towards the middle, the moderate and sober and pure, free from both vices, luxury and stinginess. Already, as we have said before, personal labor is a humble exercise, and to wash one's own feet and to anoint oneself with oil that has been poured out; and also to repay the one who anoints, in turn, and this is a communal justice, and to serve a sick friend and to help one who is not able and to offer to one who is in need. 'And Abraham placed before them', it says, 'a meal under the tree and stood by while they were eating.' And fishing, as with Peter, if we were to take a break from the necessary lessons in the word. But this is a better hunt, which the Lord gave to the disciple, teaching him to catch men, just as a fisherman catches fish through water.

pass_b_english: A gymnasium is sufficient for young men even if a bath is available, and indeed such exercises are more suitable for men before bathing; they are not worthless, since they offer something useful for the young toward health, and they instill diligence and ambition to care not only for elegance but also for soundness of soul. This is pleasant and not unprofitable when practiced without being drawn away from better works. Here too women must not be exempt from bodily exercise, yet they should not be urged to wrestling and running; rather, they should be trained in wool-working and weaving and in assisting at the spindle if needed. It is also necessary for women to fetch what we need from the storehouse themselves, and it is no shame for them to go to the mill. Nor should they fuss over their hair so that it becomes a shame to the husband and a reproach to the housekeeping wife who is his helper. If a woman also spreads a bed herself, gives a drink to her thirsty husband, and sets a meal before him, she will be exercising in a most decent and sober way for health. The Pedagogue accepts such a woman, who 'stretches out her hands to useful tasks, and her hands hold the spindle; she opens her hands to the poor, and reaches out her hands to the needy' (Prov 31:19–20). She is not ashamed to imitate Sarah in the noblest service, serving travelers. For Abraham said to her, 'Hurry and knead three measures of fine flour and make cakes' (Gen 18:6). 'And Rachel the daughter of Laban was coming with her father's sheep' (Gen 29:9), and it was not enough that she did these things; Scripture also teaches humility by adding, 'For she was shepherding her father's sheep' (Gen 29:9). The Scriptures commend many examples of frugality and personal labor together with patterns of exercise. Some men exercise naked and wrestle; others play with a small ball, enjoying the game of ball-playing in the sun; for still others, walking is enough, whether they walk toward the country or go down into the city. If they also take up a mattock, that is no ignoble accompaniment to the economic exercise of farming. I almost forgot to say that even Pittacus, the king of the Mytilenaeans, was invigorated by energetic exercise. It is also good to draw water for oneself and to cut wood for one's own use. 'And Jacob was pasturing the rest of Laban's sheep,' bearing a royal sign, 'a staff of storax,' practicing to change the nature of the wood for the better (Gen 30:37–43). For many, even reading aloud serves as exercise. And the wrestling we have approved must not be pursued for the sake of useless rivalry, but for the sake of manly, sweaty exertion—not the artificial, showy kind, but the kind that comes from upright wrestling, from the grappling of neck, hands, and sides. This sort of exertion is more decent and manly with modest strength, taken for the sake of useful and beneficial health; other gymnastic exercises betray the practice of servile postures. Everywhere one must aim at the mean. For just as it is best to regard the pains of eating as a good, so to labor beyond measure is the worst thing—troublesome and disease-producing. Therefore one must be neither completely idle nor completely exhausted. Just as we have determined concerning food, so in all things and everywhere one must not turn toward pleasure and intemperance, nor toward the opposite extreme, but toward the middle way that is harmonious, sober, and pure, free from both vices, luxury and stinginess. Already, as we said before, personal labor is a humble exercise: to put on one's own sandals, to wash one's own feet, to rub oneself with poured-out oil; and to return the same service to the one who anointed you in turn—this is the exercise of communal justice—and to attend a sick friend, to serve one who cannot help himself, and to provide for one in need. 'And Abraham set it before them,' it says, 'a meal under the tree, and he stood by them while they ate' (Gen 18:8). And fishing, as with Peter, if we take a break from the necessary lessons in the Word (Luke 5:1–11). But this is a better catch, which the Lord gave to the disciple, teaching him to catch men just as a fisherman catches fish through water.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the distinction between 'elegance' (εὐεξία) and 'soul-care' (εὐψυχία). All scriptural allusions in the Greek (Abraham, Rachel, Jacob, Peter) are correctly identified and cited in Pass B with appropriate verse numbering (Gen 18:6, Gen 29:9, Gen 30:37-43, Gen 18:8, Luke 5:1-11). The Proverbs 31:19-20 citation in Pass B is a correct identification of the quoted character description. The translation of 'ταλασιουργίᾳ' as 'wool-working' and 'ἱστουργίᾳ' as 'weaving' is accurate. The distinction between 'artificial/showy' (ἐπιδεικτικὸν) and 'upright' (ὀρθῆς) wrestling is preserved.
